summary: For children aged 7–8 (UK Year 3, US Grade 3–4) learning to write and calculate two-digit × one-digit multiplication (and matching division) by partitioning via the distributive law. The core engine is splitting a number into tens and ones, multiplying each part, and recombining — e.g. 13×4 = (10×4)+(3×4) = 40+12 = 52. The area model / grid method makes the distributive law visible as the bridge from mental partitioning to the formal written method. Guidance progresses deliberately: mental partitioning → recorded grid → expanded then compact written layout, keeping the link explicit so the written method carries meaning rather than being memorised as steps.
misconceptions: Place-value error: treating the tens digit as ones (13×4 done as 1×4 + 3×4).
Forgetting to combine ALL partial products (computing 10×4 and 3×4 but not adding them).
Multiplying digit-by-digit without regard to their place value.
Not connecting the grid/area model to the numbers (seeing it as a separate trick).
Losing the link between the mental partition and the written record, so the written method becomes meaningless steps.

activities.title: Splitting a rectangle: area model for 13×4
steps: Draw or view a rectangle 13 units wide and 4 units tall and cut it with a vertical line at the boundary between the tens and the ones, so it becomes a 10×4 piece and a 3×4 piece.
Work out the product for each piece (10×4 = 40 and 3×4 = 12) and write the number inside each region.
Add the two partial products to find the whole area: 40 + 12 = 52.

Line the grid up next to the expanded written form (40 + 12), saying which partial product matches which region of the grid. Then look at the compact column layout and explain how the 12 from 3×4 becomes 2 ones and a carried ten, which joins the 4 tens from 10×4 to make the 5 tens in 52.
Repeat with 23×4: split into 20×4 = 80 and 3×4 = 12, then combine to 92.
activities.insight: A two-digit × one-digit product is the sum of the partial products from each place-value part; the '10' in 13 contributes 10×4 = 40 (not 1×4), because you must multiply the whole value of the tens, not just its digit.

activities.title: Moving the split line — the distributive law felt as area
steps: Starting from a 13×4 rectangle already split at the tens/ones boundary, split the same rectangle (its width of 13) at a different point — for example into a 9×4 piece and a 4×4 piece (note 9 + 4 = 13, so the total width is unchanged) — and compute the two new partial products (36 and 16).
Check that whatever point you split at, the two partial products still add to the same total (52).
Discuss why the split at the tens/ones boundary is the most useful one: it uses known facts (10×4 and 3×4) and lines up with how the number is written.
State the rule in words: splitting the rectangle into parts and adding the parts' areas always gives the whole area.
activities.insight: The product is unchanged by how you partition — the distributive law — and partitioning by place value is chosen because it lands on known facts and matches the written numerals.

activities.title: Linking multiplication to division with known facts
steps: Write the division that matches a multiplication fact you have made (e.g. from 10×4 = 40 write 40÷4 = 10).
Solve 96 ÷ 8 by partitioning: split 96 into 80 + 16, divide each by 8 (80÷8 = 10, 16÷8 = 2) and recombine to get 12.
Alternatively, ask 'what times 8 is near 96?' and use the known fact 8×12 = 96.
Check the answer by multiplying back: 8×12 = 80 + 16 = 96.
activities.insight: Division can be reached through known multiplication facts and the same place-value partitioning, so multiplication and division are two views of the same relationship.

activities.title: Grid-to-written-method reference and check
steps: Given a completed grid, fill in each partial product and then the total, then write the same calculation in the expanded form (e.g. 40 + 12) and the compact column form.
Match a grid diagram to the written calculation that goes with it.
Tackle a check question with the common trap answer present — for 13×4, explain why 16 is wrong (it comes from 1×4 + 3×4, treating the tens digit as ones) and why 52 is right.
Point to each region of a grid and say where its partial product appears in the expanded written method, and how it contributes (including any carry) to the compact form.
activities.insight: Each step of the written method corresponds to a region of the grid; spotting the place-value trap answer shows understanding of why the tens must be multiplied as tens.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to work these while you watch the method: 23 × 4 (encourage partitioning aloud), and 96 ÷ 8 using facts they know. Watch how they break 23 into 20 and 3, whether they multiply BOTH parts, and how they recombine.
checkAnswer: 23 × 4 = 92 (20×4 = 80, 3×4 = 12, 80 + 12 = 92). 96 ÷ 8 = 12 (e.g. 80÷8 = 10 and 16÷8 = 2, or knows 8×12 = 96). The teacher watches for partitioning by place value, multiplying every part, and recombining — not just multiplying the tens digit.
